The secret ballot is a way of voting in which no one can see or find out how a person voted. Its modern form, a government-printed paper listing all candidates and marked in private, was introduced in 1856 by the Australian colonies of Victoria and South Australia, which is why it was long called the "Australian ballot".

Before it, voting was often public. In Britain and its colonies voters called out their choice at the hustings, or handed in party-printed tickets that everyone could recognise. Landlords, employers and party agents could see who voted which way, which made bribery and intimidation easy. The British Chartists had demanded the ballot since the 1830s.

What the Australian design added:

  • One official ballot paper, printed at public cost, with every candidate's name.
  • A private booth or screen where the voter marks it.
  • A sealed box, and counting without any way to link a paper to a voter.

Victoria was booming from the gold rush, full of new migrants with radical ideas about democracy, and adopted the system in March 1856, followed by South Australia within weeks. Britain followed with the Ballot Act of 1872, and most American states in the 1880s and 1890s. Today it is a basic standard of free elections worldwide.

It made voting by the poor and dependent safer, and it fitted the wider push for broad suffrage in the Australian and New Zealand colonies, which led to votes for women in 1893. A few places still vote in public by choice, such as the open-air assemblies of some Swiss cantons.
